facts.fact_text: The applicants are members of EĞİTİM-SEN (Eğitim ve Bilim Emekçileri Sendikası – The Education Workers' Trade Union).
EĞİTİM-SEN (Eğitim ve Bilim Emekçileri Sendikası – The Education Workers' Trade Union) is a trade union.
On 18 December 2000, the Governorship of Ankara issued a circular providing guidelines on meetings and demonstrations organised in the city of Ankara.

According to the circular issued by the Governorship of Ankara on 18 December 2000, the meeting place chosen by KESK (Kamu Emekçileri Sendikaları Konfederasyonu – The Confederation of Public Employees' Trade Unions) was not among the permitted areas.

On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), while the president of KESK (Kamu Emekçileri Sendikaları Konfederasyonu – The Confederation of Public Employees' Trade Unions) was reading out press statements, police officers warned the demonstrators that their action was contrary to the law.

On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), while the president of KESK (Kamu Emekçileri Sendikaları Konfederasyonu – The Confederation of Public Employees' Trade Unions) was reading out press statements, police officers warned the demonstrators that they had to disperse.
On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), the demonstrators blocked the main street of the Kızılay district (Atatürk Avenue).
On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), the demonstrators attempted to march towards the Prime Minister's Office.
On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), police officers intervened and used truncheons with a view to dispersing the crowds.
On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), police officers intervened and used sticks with a view to dispersing the crowds.
On both occasions (7 June 2001 and 25 June 2001), police officers intervened and used tear gas with a view to dispersing the crowds.

On 26 June 2001, the Ankara public prosecutor brought charges against twenty-seven demonstrators, including Arzu Doğan and Sami Evren, for violation of the Law on Meetings and Demonstration Marches (Law no. 2911).

On 23 July 2001, pursuant to Law no. 4483 on the prosecution of civil servants, the Ankara public prosecutor transferred the file to the Ministry of Interior seeking an authorisation to initiate criminal proceedings.
On 9 October 2001, the Ministry of the Interior decided not to take action against the officials and officers accused by the applicants.

On 29 January 2002, the Ankara public prosecutor issued a decision of non-prosecution as regards the applicants' complaints against the Ankara Governor, the director of the Ankara Security Directorate, the director of the Rapid Intervention Force branch of the Ankara Security Directorate, and the police officers involved in the incidents.
The circular issued by the Governorship of Ankara on 18 December 2000 was issued in accordance with the Law on Meetings and Demonstration Marches (Law no. 2911).
Article 34 of the Turkish Constitution provides that everyone has the right to hold unarmed and peaceful meetings and demonstration marches without prior permission.

Article 34 of the Turkish Constitution provides that the formalities, conditions, and procedures governing the exercise of the right to hold meetings and demonstration marches shall be prescribed by law.

At the material time, section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) required that, in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting.

At the material time, section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) required that the notification to the governor's office or district authorities must be by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising board.
Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) prohibited demonstrations and processions on public streets.
Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) prohibited demonstrations and processions in parks.
Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) prohibited demonstrations and processions in places of worship.
Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) prohibited demonstrations and processions in buildings in which public services were based.

Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) required that demonstrations organised in public squares comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.

Section 24 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) provided that demonstrations and processions which did not comply with the provisions of the Act would be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators had been warned.

Article 16(a) of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that the police may use firearms in the event of self-defence.

Article 16(h) of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that the police may use firearms if a person or a group resists the police and prevents them from carrying out their duties or if there is an attack against the police.

Additional Article 6 (dated 16 June 1985) of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that in cases of resistance by persons whose arrest is necessary or by groups whose dispersal is necessary, or of their threatening to attack or carrying out an attack, the police may use violence to subdue these actions.

Additional Article 6 (dated 16 June 1985) of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that use of violence refers to the use of bodily force, physical force and all types of weapons specified in the law, and it gradually increases according to the nature and level of resistance and attack in such a way as to restore calm.

Additional Article 6 (dated 16 June 1985) of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police provides that in cases of intervention by group forces, the extent of the use of force and the equipment and instruments to be used are determined by the commander of the intervening force.

The Ministry of the Interior considered that the police officers had been under an obligation to disperse the demonstrators who had organised an illegal meeting.
